title: Producing algorithms: pseudocode
starter: Write instructions for making a cup of tea so precise that someone who has never seen a kettle could follow them.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: What pseudocode is
facts: Pseudocode describes an algorithm in a structured, language-free way.
It cannot be run: it is written for a human reader, not a computer.
It lets you plan the logic before choosing a language.
stations.challenge: Explain why pseudocode is written even though it cannot be run.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Pseudocode describes an algorithm in a structured, language-free way.
Also credit: It cannot be run: it is written for a human reader, not a computer.

questions.a: A structured way of writing an algorithm for a human reader, not tied to one language
You can get the logic right without fighting the syntax of a language

stations.name: Variables and assignment
facts: A variable is a named place to store a value that can change.
Assignment puts a value into a variable: total = 0.
In the reference language, input is written name = input('...') and output is print(...).
stations.challenge: Write three lines of pseudocode that input a name and greet the user.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A variable is a named place to store a value that can change.
Also credit: Assignment puts a value into a variable: total = 0.

questions.a: Takes the current value of total, adds one, and stores the result back in total

questions.q: Which line correctly inputs a number and stores it?

stations.name: Selection
facts: Selection chooses between paths using if, elseif and else.
In the reference language a block ends with endif.
stations.challenge: Write pseudocode that reports whether a mark is a pass or a fail.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Selection chooses between paths using if, elseif and else.
Also credit: The condition uses comparison operators: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=.

questions.q: What is the difference between = and == ?
questions.a: One equals sign assigns a value; two compare two values

questions.q: Put these lines into the right order for a grading algorithm.
questions.a: if mark >= 70 then →   print('Distinction') → elseif mark >= 50 then →   print('Merit') → else →   print('Pass') → endif

stations.name: Iteration
facts: Iteration repeats steps. A for loop repeats a known number of times.
A while loop repeats as long as a condition is true, and may never run at all.
A do-until loop always runs at least once, then checks.
stations.challenge: Write a loop that prints the numbers one to five.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Iteration repeats steps. A for loop repeats a known number of times.
Also credit: A while loop repeats as long as a condition is true, and may never run at all.

questions.q: When would you choose a while loop rather than a for loop?
questions.a: When you don't know in advance how many repeats are needed

questions.q: How many times does 'for i = 1 to 5' run its body?

stations.name: Arrays and subprograms
facts: An array holds several values under one name, numbered from zero.
scores[0] is the first item, scores[1] the second.
A subprogram is defined with function or procedure and called by name.
stations.challenge: Write pseudocode that outputs the third item of an array called names.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: An array holds several values under one name, numbered from zero.
Also credit: scores[0] is the first item, scores[1] the second.

questions.q: An array called names holds ['Ash','Bea','Cal']. What does names[1] give?
What is the difference between a function and a procedure?
questions.a: A function returns a value; a procedure does not

stations.name: Reading the reference language
facts: The exam uses OCR's own reference language, close to Python but not identical.
You are never asked to write in a specific language: any clear pseudocode is accepted.
You do need to read the reference language accurately.
stations.challenge: Read a short reference-language program and state its output.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: The exam uses OCR's own reference language, close to Python but not identical.
Also credit: You are never asked to write in a specific language: any clear pseudocode is accepted.

questions.q: What does this print: total = 0; for i = 1 to 4; total = total + i; next i; print(total)?
In the exam, which language must you write your answer in?
questions.a: Any language or clear pseudocode: the logic is what is marked

final.name: Final challenge: read the code

questions.q: What does this program output?  n = 5 · r = 1 · while n > 1: r = r * n, n = n - 1 · print(r)
What does this output?  a = [3, 9, 4] · t = 0 · for i = 0 to 2: t = t + a[i] · print(t / 3)
Put these lines into a working program that counts down from 3 to 1.
questions.a: n = 3 → while n > 0 →   print(n) →   n = n - 1 → endwhile

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: State what is meant by pseudocode.
points: Pseudocode describes an algorithm in a structured, language-free way.
You are never asked to write in a specific language: any clear pseudocode is accepted.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
